newsitem.title: USA: U.S. beef output seen flat in '97, down in '98.
newsitem.headline: U.S. beef output seen flat in '97, down in '98.

text.p: A top livestock analyst at the U.S. Agriculture Department forecast U.S. beef production would be "little changed" in 1997 from the prior year and that output would decline in 1998 and 1999.

"Sharp drops in beef output are likely next year following the downturn in cattle inventories we are now seeing," USDA analyst James Nix said in a speech prepared for delivery on Tuesday at USDA's annual Agricultural Outlook Forum.
Nix said a higher percentage of 1997's output would come from fed beef as slaughter of feedlot cattle increases and cow slaughter drops sharply.
He said production would likely drop four to five percent in 1998 with both fed beef output and cow beef production falling and said further declines are likely in 1999.
Total cattle and calves inventory will slip lower in 1997 with the Jan. 1, 1998 inventory posting a decline of about three percent and continuing to decrease in 1998, he said.

Feeder cattle supplies will tighten further in 1997, primarily because of the smaller calf crop expected, as well as slowing imports from Mexico. They will continue to tighten in 1998 as the calf crop slips from the 1997 level.
Nix said the average weight of cattle slaughtered will probably continue to trend upward for at least several years.
For all 1997, beef exports are expected to increase 10 percent from the 1996 level.

"Growth in demand for high quality beef in the major importing countries of the world, particularly the biggest customers for U.S. beef, are expected to support the continued climb in beef exports," the speech said.

Concerns over BSE and E.coli hurts exports to top customer Japan in 1996 and, while those concerns are expected to moderate, likely continued strength of the dollar against the yen may have a dampening affect on exports in 1997.
Exports to Korea and Mexico will likely exhibit continued strength, however exports to Canada are expected to be lower in 1997 after being off in 1996, the analyst said.
On imports, Nix said declining U.S. cow beef supplies and weakness in the Japanese market will likely result in larger supplies entering the U.S. market in 1997.

In the speech, Nix said fed cattle prices are expected remain under pressure into the spring but are seen rising in the second half of 1997 and in 1998. An increase is also seen in feeder cattle prices in 1997 and likely again in 1998.

Nix said the forecasts were the product of USDA's Meat Animals and Poultry Interagency Commodity Estimates Committees and might differ from those in USDA's Baseline forecasts because they were based on newer data.
